$comment: The release manifest. A running nudo fetches this to tell you when there is
a newer version, and renders `notes` as the in-app changelog.
Publishing a release is a commit to this file — no CDN, no bespoke service.
The workflow in .github/workflows/release.yml adds an entry on tag push.
Set `breaking` when a release needs manual steps; the dashboard shows those
differently, because the whole point of a changelog is that someone reads the

releases.notes:
Self-upgrade now takes one switch instead of two. The NUDO_ALLOW_SELF_UPGRADE
environment variable is gone; the toggle in settings is the whole gate.

The flag assumed whoever installs an instance and whoever operates it are
different people who should each have to say yes. For a tool one person runs on
their own box that was a second lock on the same door, and its only visible
effect was a dashboard refusing an upgrade someone had already opted into.

Nothing about the safety of the path changed: the release is still verified
against the digest published in this manifest, still staged beside the running
one, and still reverted by nudo-boot-guard if the new version cannot start.
Containers and flat /usr/local/bin installs are still refused.

If you installed 0.4.0 and set NUDO_ALLOW_SELF_UPGRADE in your unit, it is now
ignored and can be removed.

### Fixed

- Stop filing merged pull requests under "Other"

### Other

- Self-updating binary install: upgrade from the dashboard (#9)

### Added

- **Custom domains and automatic HTTPS.** Give a service a domain and it is
  served over HTTPS with a valid certificate. nudo installs and manages Caddy
  as a systemd unit on the target; certificates are Caddy's problem entirely,
  so nudo implements no ACME and never handles a private key for one.

      nudo targets ingress enable tgt_abc --acme-email ops@example.com
      nudo services domain svc_abc --route api.example.com:8080

  Point an A record at the target and that is the whole of it.

- **A service can answer on several addresses.** An apex and its `www`, a
  public domain and an internal one, or a path under a domain whose root is
  served by something else. A path is stripped before the request reaches the
  service, so a service routed at `/api` sees `/users` rather than
  `/api/users`.

      nudo services domain svc_1 --route example.com:8080 \
                                 --route www.example.com:8080
      nudo services domain svc_api --route example.com/api:9090

- **gRPC.** A gRPC server needs HTTP/2 end to end; a proxy that downgrades to
  HTTP/1.1 breaks every call, silently, in a way that looks like the service
  being at fault. Pass `--grpc` and the proxy reaches it over cleartext HTTP/2
  with TLS at the edge.

      nudo services domain svc_grpc --route grpc.example.com:50051 --grpc

- **`nudo targets ingress check`** diagnoses the failure this feature actually
  has: a domain whose DNS does not point at the target yet cannot be issued a
  certificate, and Caddy retries indefinitely without saying so anywhere
  obvious. It is reported as a warning rather than a failure, since the record
  may be minutes away.

- **Bring your own proxy.** `--mode external` renders the config from your
  services' domains and never touches the host, for an existing nginx or
  Traefik you are not giving up.

### Notes

- Nothing that predates this release becomes reachable by domain. Every
  existing service reads as not routed, which is what is true of all of them
  today, and every existing target as having no ingress.
- A rejected proxy config does not fail the deploy that triggered it. The
  service is up and healthy and the proxy keeps serving its previous routes —
  Caddy restores them itself. The target is marked degraded with the reason,
  which is worth knowing because a degraded proxy is easy to miss precisely
  because the site still works.
- Enabling ingress on a latency-critical target needs
  `--allow-latency-critical`, like every other mutation of such a host. A
  reverse proxy adds a hop to every request and a process competing for CPU
  and cache.
- Two services on one target claiming the same port is now refused, naming the
  service that already holds it. One service may reuse its own port across
  several routes.
- Raw TCP and UDP are not supported: Caddy needs a plugin that is not in the
  standard binary for those. A service that is neither HTTP nor gRPC still
  needs its port reached directly.

### Security

- SSH host keys are verified. `check_server_key` previously returned true
  unconditionally, so every host key was accepted every time — and nudo holds
  the private key for every target it manages, so anything able to answer for
  a target's address was handed an authentication attempt with that key. Keys
  are now trusted on first use and checked on every connection after that,
  during the handshake, so an unrecognised host is refused before
  authentication.
- A changed host key is recorded rather than only reported. Review both
  fingerprints on the target's page, or run
  `nudo targets host-key <id> --accept <fingerprint>`. Accepting names the
  fingerprint, so a key that changes again in between is refused.

### Added

- Builds can run on a host other than the control plane. Register one with
  `nudo build-hosts add`, or from Build hosts in the dashboard, then point a
  service at it or set an instance-wide default. The checkout is cloned on the
  build host itself, so the control plane no longer needs the toolchain — or
  the CPU — for a build. A build host's host key is pinned on the same terms
  as a target's.
- `nudo secrets rotate` replaces the value of a secret that already exists.

### Changed

- Storing a secret on a name that is already taken is refused rather than
  silently overwriting it. A secret's value cannot be read back, so the old
  one was unrecoverable. Use `nudo secrets rotate` — or the Rotate button on
  the dashboard — to replace one deliberately.
- The repository's module layout was reworked. No behaviour change beyond the
  four fixes recorded in CHANGES.md, the notable one being that masked target
  and service updates are now atomic.

### Notes

- Nothing that predates this release builds anywhere new: a service with no
  build host set keeps building on the control plane.
- A build host shared with latency-sensitive workloads is allowed, and warned
  about rather than refused.
- If a target's host key has changed since you last deployed, the first
  connection after upgrading will stop and ask you to review it.
